title: How do you induct new board directors?
seoTitle: How to induct new board directors
description: How to induct new board directors: assess each director's gaps, cover duties, business, risk and governance, set a timeline, and evidence completion.
shortAnswer: Induct new board directors by assessing each director's existing knowledge against what the role requires, then delivering a tailored program covering legal duties, the organization's business model and strategy, risk profile, governance arrangements, financial statements and key regulatory obligations. Combine an information pack, briefings with senior executives and site visits, set a timeline with milestones, and record what was covered so the board can show the director was equipped to perform the role.
keyTakeaways: Governance codes and regulators expect a formal induction. The ASX Corporate Governance Principles say listed entities should have a program for inducting new directors, and EU banking guidelines set induction timelines.
Tailor induction to the individual. The ASX commentary adds legal duties and accounting training where a director lacks them.
EU suitability guidelines for banks and investment firms expect key information within one month of appointment and induction completed within six months.
Induction is the start of ongoing development, not a one off event. Boards should periodically review whether directors need further professional development.
Keep a record of the induction plan, what was delivered and any agreed follow up, because regulators may ask how a director was prepared.

blocks.text: Directors carry legal duties from the day they are appointed, so induction is how an organization makes sure a new director can meet them quickly. Governance codes and financial regulators treat it as part of board effectiveness, and some regulators assess whether it happened.

In Australia, for example, Recommendation 2.6 of the ASX Corporate Governance Council's Corporate Governance Principles and Recommendations (fourth edition, 2019) says a listed entity "should have a program for inducting new directors and for periodically reviewing whether there is a need for existing directors to undertake professional development" ([ASX, fourth edition](https://www.asx.com.au/content/dam/asx/about/corporate-governance-council/cgc-principles-and-recommendations-fourth-edn.pdf)). Listed entities report against the recommendations on an if not, why not basis. As at November 2026 the fourth edition remains current; ASX consulted on a draft fifth edition from July 21 to September 14, 2026 ([ASX](https://www.asx.com.au/about/regulation/asx-corporate-governance-council)).

In the European Union, the Capital Requirements Directive requires institutions within its scope to devote adequate human and financial resources to the induction and training of management body members, and the 2024 amendments (Directive (EU) 2024/1619) extend this to include environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks and impacts and information and communication technology (ICT) risk ([Directive 2013/36/EU](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32013L0036); [Directive (EU) 2024/1619](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024L1619); see [EBA internal governance and staff training](/regulations/eba-internal-governance-staff-training)).

sections.heading: What should a director induction cover?

blocks.text: Cover the director's legal duties, the organization's business and strategy, its risk profile, its governance arrangements, its financial position, and the director's own role on the board and committees. The joint European Banking Authority (EBA) and European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) suitability guidelines describe the purpose as facilitating a clear understanding of relevant laws and regulations, the institution's structure, business model, risk profile and governance arrangements, and the member's role within them ([EBA/GL/2021/06, paragraph 92](https://www.eba.europa.eu/sites/default/files/document_library/Publications/Guidelines/2021/EBA-GL-2021-06%20Joint%20GLs%20on%20the%20assessment%20of%20suitability%20%28fit%26propoer%29/1022127/Final%20report%20on%20joint%20EBA%20and%20ESMA%20GL%20on%20the%20assessment%20of%20suitability.pdf)).

sections.heading: How do you tailor the induction to each director?

blocks.text: Start with a gap assessment against the knowledge the role and the board's skills matrix require, then build the program around the gaps. The ASX commentary says all new directors should be offered induction training "tailored to their existing skills, knowledge and experience," and that it should include training on legal duties for directors unfamiliar with the legal framework and on key accounting matters and financial statement responsibilities for directors without accounting skills.

The EBA and ESMA guidelines make the same point for financial institutions: where a member needs to fill a gap in required knowledge and skills, training should aim to fill it within an appropriate timeframe, where possible before the member takes up the position, and in any case all required knowledge and skill elements should be met within one year of taking up the position (paragraph 94). Record the assessment, the agreed program and the target dates, using the same logic as a [training gap analysis](/guides/how-to-run-a-training-gap-analysis).

items: Ask the new director to self assess against the board skills matrix, and have the chair or nomination committee validate it.
Separate items every director receives from items specific to this director.
Give sector newcomers more time on business and regulatory context; give experienced sector directors more time on this organization's specific risks and culture.
Agree a mentor or buddy director for the first board cycle.

sections.heading: What timeline should a director induction follow?

blocks.text: Front load what the director needs for their first meetings and complete the full program within a set period. The EBA and ESMA guidelines expect newly appointed management body members to receive key information within one month of taking up the position and to complete induction within six months (paragraph 93). The plan below is illustrative and fits within those limits.

sections.heading: What policy and records should support director induction?

blocks.text: Adopt a written induction and training policy, resource it, and keep records that show it was followed. The EBA and ESMA guidelines expect institutions to have policies and procedures for induction and training adopted by the management body, with objectives, responsibilities, resources and a clear process for any member to request induction or training (paragraphs 95 to 97), a process to identify training needs collectively and individually (paragraph 99), and an evaluation process to review the quality of induction and training provided (paragraph 101).

Outside financial services, regulators still expect directors to know their duties. Australia's charity regulator, the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission (ACNC), suggests steps such as outlining duties in a letter of appointment, regularly providing information or training on duties, and requesting that responsible persons undertake relevant training ([ACNC](https://www.acnc.gov.au/for-charities/manage-your-charity/governance-hub/governance-standards); see [ACNC governance standards and board duties](/regulations/acnc-governance-standards-board-duties)).

items: The induction plan and gap assessment for each director.
A log of sessions, presenters, dates and materials provided.
Training records for targeted training, including regulator mandated topics, such as management body training under [NIS2](/regulations/nis2-management-body-training) where it applies.
The completion review and the ongoing development plan.
Periodic reporting to the board or nomination committee on director development, as covered in [reporting training compliance to the board](/guides/how-to-report-training-compliance-to-the-board).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents a board's required knowledge, from legal duties to the organization's principal risks, as defined concepts linked to their sources, so each director's gap assessment, induction sessions and later development can be mapped to the same structure and evidenced. See [knowledge governance](/platform/knowledge-governance) and [financial services](/industries/financial-services).

faqs.q: How long should a director induction take?
faqs.a: There is no universal rule. For EU banks and investment firms, the EBA and ESMA suitability guidelines expect key information within one month and induction completed within six months of taking up the position. Many organizations outside that scope use a similar three to six month program, front loaded before the first board meetings.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for director induction?
faqs.a: The chair usually owns it, with the company secretary organizing it. The ASX Principles list helping to organize and facilitate the induction and professional development of directors among the company secretary's roles. A nomination committee often approves the policy and reviews completion.

faqs.q: Do experienced directors still need an induction?
faqs.a: Yes, though it should be shorter and different. Experience elsewhere does not cover this organization's strategy, risks, culture, governance arrangements or open regulatory issues. The ASX commentary specifically calls for induction tailored to each director's existing skills, knowledge and experience.

It depends on the entity and jurisdiction. The ASX recommendation applies on an if not, why not basis. For institutions within the scope of the EU Capital Requirements Directive, the directive requires adequate resources for induction and training, and the EBA and ESMA guidelines set expectations that supervisors use in suitability assessments. Check the rules for your sector.
